title: string: a special type
sub: A reference type that behaves like a value
cards/0/body:
string is a reference type: the text lives on the heap. But a string is immutable. Any "edit" creates a new string, and the old one stays exactly as it was.

That's why strings are safe to pass anywhere: nobody can mess up your text.
cards/1/task: Step through and see what += does.
cards/1/steps/0/note: The string "kit" is on the heap; a holds a reference.
cards/1/steps/1/note: b leads to the same string.
cards/1/steps/2/note: += doesn't change "kit": a new string "kitten" is created, and b now leads to it.
cards/2/explain: The string "kit" didn't change. b got a reference to a new string; a didn't.
cards/3/q: Two strings with the same text were built in different ways. What does a == b return?
cards/3/explain: The == operator on string compares text, not references. These are different objects, but the text is the same.
cards/4/title: Concatenating strings in a loop is a bad idea
cards/4/body:
s += x in a loop creates a new string every time and copies all the accumulated text into it. 10,000 iterations means 10,000 garbage strings and work that grows quadratically.

StringBuilder collects text in a mutable buffer and builds the string once at the end.
cards/5/q: How many new strings does this loop create?
cards/5/explain: Each += creates a new string. The literal "x" is only one object, though: it's interned.
cards/6/body:
Identical string literals in a program are one and the same object: the CLR keeps them in the intern pool.

Strings built at run time don't go there unless you call string.Intern.
cards/6/deep: That's why ReferenceEquals("abc", "abc") is usually true, but false for a string with the same text from a StringBuilder. Comparing strings by reference is a bug: use == or string.Equals with the right StringComparison.
cards/7/q: What is true about string? Select all that apply.
cards/7/options/1: Once created, a string can't be changed
cards/7/options/3: The string's text lives on the stack
cards/7/explain: Replace, ToUpper and other methods return a new string. If you don't keep the result, nothing changes.
cards/8/q: Build a fast way to join words
cards/8/explain: StringBuilder.Append writes into the buffer without creating intermediate strings.
